prompt.context: Your client is a pharmaceutical product manufacturer of over-the-counter (OTC) drugs. They have two product lines: a big line (Product A) and a small line (Product B). Trends in both the industry and the company are uninspiring — growth is flat and costs are creeping upward.
prompt.question: Profitability has been declining. Diagnose the problem and recommend what the client should do.

clarifying_info.q: Can you confirm that declining profitability is the core issue?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, flat growth combined with rising costs means profitability is declining.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market size and our share for each product?
clarifying_info.a: Product A total market is $1.2B; our share is one-third (i.e., ~$400M). Product B total market is $700M; our revenue is $150M.

clarifying_info.q: How has market share been trending?
clarifying_info.a: Share is flat. Market is also flat.

clarifying_info.q: Are there competitors, and are they gaining share?
clarifying_info.a: All things are constant — share and market are both flat.

clarifying_info.q: What is in the product pipeline?
clarifying_info.a: Nothing notable in the pipeline; growth prospects are uninspiring.

clarifying_info.q: What are the gross margins and fixed costs for each product?
clarifying_info.a: Product A has a gross margin of 40% and fixed costs of $180M. Product B has a gross margin of 60% and fixed costs of $70M.

framework: Revenue side: market size × market share for each product; check for pricing power, pipeline, geographic expansion
Cost side: split fixed (R&D, production, labor, manufacturing overhead) vs. variable (raw materials, distribution)
Assess each product's contribution independently before looking at combined P&L
After diagnosing, explore options to restore profitability (revenue levers, cost cuts, synergies, M&A, divestiture)

questions.prompt: Calculate the net operating profit (gross profit minus fixed costs) for each product.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply revenue by gross margin to get gross profit, then subtract fixed costs to arrive at net operating contribution. A clear table layout is expected.

math.setup: Product A revenue = $1.2B × (1/3) = $400M; gross margin = 40%; fixed costs = $180M. Product B revenue = $150M; gross margin = 60%; fixed costs = $70M.
math.answer: Product A is losing $20M; Product B is making $20M; combined break-even.

questions.prompt: What options exist to improve Product A's profitability? Evaluate each.
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm revenue-side and cost-side levers: increase prices, sell more volume, launch new SKUs, find synergies with Product B, expand geographically, acquire a competitor to gain scale. Interviewer should guide candidate to recognize all options are difficult or unavailable in this flat market.

questions.prompt: How much additional revenue would Product A need to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should work backward from the $20M loss using the gross margin to determine the required incremental revenue.

math.setup: Product A is losing $20M. To break even, gross profit must increase by $20M. With a 40% gross margin, incremental revenue needed = $20M / 40%.
math.answer: Product A would need an additional $50M in revenue to break even.

questions.prompt: Given that no revenue or cost improvement options are viable, what is your recommendation?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recommend shutting down Product A as the last-resort option. This should only be reached after systematically exhausting all other alternatives — it demonstrates rigorous analysis rather than jumping to an easy answer.

brainstorming.prompt: If the client wants to avoid shutting down Product A, what levers could they pull to increase revenue or reduce costs?

categories.name: Revenue — Volume
ideas: Increase marketing spend to gain share in flat market

categories.name: Revenue — Pricing
ideas: Raise OTC drug prices (check elasticity and regulatory constraints)
Bundle Product A with Product B for premium pricing

categories.name: Revenue — Product
ideas: Diversify the product line with adjacent OTC SKUs
Leverage the existing brand for line extensions

categories.name: Cost — Fixed
ideas: Consolidate manufacturing facilities with Product B
Reduce R&D spend if no pipeline

categories.name: Cost — Variable
ideas: Renegotiate raw material contracts at scale
Optimize distribution routes to reduce logistics cost

categories.name: Strategic
ideas: Acquire a competitor to gain economies of scale for Product A
License out Product A brand to a third party
Find synergies between Product A and Product B production lines

recommendation: Shut down Product A — it is losing $20M per year and no viable path to profitability exists given flat market share, flat market growth, and no pipeline
Retain Product B, which is profitable at +$20M net
Reinvest resources freed from Product A into strengthening Product B or exploring new product development
risks: Shutdown costs (inventory write-downs, severance, facility costs) could be significant
Loss of Product A may reduce negotiating leverage with distributors who carry both lines
Brand equity of the OTC portfolio may weaken without a flagship big-line product
next_steps: Model the one-time shutdown costs to assess payback period
Evaluate whether Product B margins can absorb any shared overhead previously allocated to Product A
Explore whether Product A assets (brand, manufacturing capacity) can be divested rather than simply shut down
